title: 01 - Political Theory: Meaning & Approaches

content.text: Syllabus — Political Theory: meaning and approaches. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 1)

meaning, nature, scope and contents of political theory; political theory as history / philosophy / science; the debate on the decline and resurgence of political theory; and approaches — Traditional (philosophical/normative, historical, empirical, legal, institutional), Modern (behavioural, post-behavioural, systems) and Contemporary/Other (postmodern, textual & contextual, deconstruction).

Define political theory → show what it is made of → prove it still matters.

Its nature is a triple identity: it is
in so far as it rests on facts,

in so far as it explains — hence the theorist must be ‘part historian, part philosopher, part scientist’.

— that India is a parliamentary democracy resting on universal adult franchise;

A theory is dispassionate and disinterested, asking whether an arrangement of power is just; an ideology — like a party manifesto — begins by assuming its own side is right and reasons backwards, its author being an ‘interested party’. This distinction preserves political theory’s claim to objectivity.

Far from being escapist, political theory alone addresses questions no quantity of data can settle — reservation, euthanasia, the use of AI in adjudication. It yields not merely a theory of man or society but a

Political theory has grown from its normative past to its scientific present and now seeks a synthesis of history, philosophy and science, of normativism and empiricism. Its relevance lies in being a practical, action-guiding activity;

The normative approach keeps values at the centre of the discipline. Empirical enquiry ‘strengthens our means’, but we must resort to political philosophy ‘to determine our ends’ — engineering can build the car, but never choose the destination. Q — Examine the importance of the behavioural approach in political theory. What led to its decline? (UPSC 2021)
Two parts — first the achievements of behaviouralism, then the reasons it declined.
— make politics a science by studying actual behaviour, not institutions.
(Not “what does the Constitution say?” but “why did this voter choose this party?”)
8 tenets (regularities, systematisation, technique, measurement, verification, integration, value-neutrality, pure science).
— arrested PT’s decline; pioneered electoral studies (psephology); made comparative politics real — in developing states ‘text differs from context’
(the Constitution promises equality; the village practises caste)
— ignoring values is like “making no difference between pure and dirty water.”
himself admitted scholars sat in ‘ivory towers’ while the 1960s civil-rights, women’s and anti-war movements raged.
— a necessary corrective, but its blindness to values caused the ‘second decline’ → post-behaviouralism (1969).

Behaviouralism was the attempt to turn politics into a science by studying how people actually behave, using data and remaining value-neutral. Instead of asking what the Constitution prescribes, it asks why a particular voter chose a particular party — dissolving formal institutions into ‘systems’ and ‘processes’ to focus on the conduct of real actors.
Though it flourished among American scholars after the Second World War, it began with
— regularities, systematisation, technique, measurement, verification, integration, value-neutrality and pure science.
Behaviouralism arrested the decline of the discipline. It pioneered the study of
, giving parties a scientific basis for strategy; it clarified the gap between theory and practice, as elitists and pluralists tested the reality of democracy in the West; and it made

a major field by showing that in developing societies ‘text differs from context’ — the Constitution promises equality while the village practises caste — so legal-institutional study alone was inadequate.

, argued that a value-free science destroys the distinction between higher and lower ends: ignoring values is like “making no difference between pure water and dirty water.” Others denied that regularities are even possible in human conduct, since the same person may not behave alike twice in like conditions.
By chasing measurement and method, behaviouralism sacrificed both the scope and the relevance of the subject.

himself conceded that scholars were “sitting in ivory towers, perfecting their techniques” while ignoring the purposes they served. The upheavals of the 1950s–60s — civil rights, the women’s movement, Vietnam — exposed a discipline with nothing to offer policymakers, triggering the post-behavioural revolution of 1969.

Behaviouralism was a necessary corrective that made political science rigorous and empirical; but its indifference to values produced a ‘second decline’, out of which post-behaviouralism emerged as a synthesis rather than a rejection.

Its watchword was that “it is better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.” Easton called for a

Easton’s features follow from this: it does not reject values but
them; theory must have the capacity to solve crises; it should promote values that help civilisation flourish; political science is an

Traditionalism is the thesis, behaviouralism the antithesis, and post-behaviouralism the

a rejection of behaviouralism: its assumptions, methods and approaches remain the same, and only two things change — technique may be compromised for the sake of relevance, and values are readmitted. It keeps the microscope, but insists on studying disease rather than dust. Where behaviouralism sought pure knowledge, micro-level and indifferent to change, post-behaviouralism seeks applied knowledge, macro-level and committed to social problem-solving.
By restoring the normative dimension without abandoning scientific method, post-behaviouralism reconciled facts and values and paved the way for the resurgence of political theory.

Q — “Political theory is dead.” Critically examine the debate on the decline of political theory. What, according to David Easton, were its causes? (UPSC 2018)
State the ‘death’ charge → give Easton’s four causes → add the other critics → judge whether it really died.
: traditional PT is ‘mere speculation’, devoid of observation of political reality.
— living ‘parasitically on ideas a century old’.
(Teaching Plato and Aristotle while unable to explain the rise of fascism.)
— values excluded in the chase for a value-neutral science.
‘theoretical malnutrition and a surfeit of facts’.
(irrelevant in both capitalist and communist systems),
(the ‘good society’ already achieved in the US),
(positivism ‘obliterates the distinction between men and brutes’).
— not death but an eclipse of the normative side; even Cobban said ‘all was not yet lost’, and Easton himself launched the revival in 1969.
In the 1950s the exponents of the ‘new science of politics’ declared traditional political theory to be in decline.
The Political System: An Inquiry into the State of Political Science (1953)
, asserted that it rested on “mere speculation” and was devoid of acute observation of political reality; to lay scientific foundations, politics had to be rescued from the study of the classics.
Easton’s first cause: historicists such as

dwelt on century-old ideas, making the discipline ‘parasitic’ and blind to contemporary problems — political scientists were expounding Plato and Aristotle while unable to account for the rise of fascism or communism.

The second cause was the exclusion of value from political theory in pursuit of the empirical scientist’s value-neutrality. Easton himself did not favour abandoning values altogether: a value system sensitive to society’s problems is necessary, and its abandonment in the name of science impoverished the discipline.
The third cause was the over-reliance on scientific method, whereby
method was given primacy over purpose
— an obsession with facts and information, captured in

“we want facts, facts and facts.” Political scientists grew adept at measuring opinion and voting yet gave their research no theoretical dimension, a condition Easton called ‘theoretical malnutrition and a surfeit of facts’.
) argued theory had lost significance in capitalist systems dominated by bureaucracy and in communist systems ruled by a party oligarchy.
) claimed the age-old search for the ‘good society’ had ended in the United States, which was “the closest approximation to the good society in operation.”
replied that the new science of politics was itself a symptom of decline: by adopting positivism it ignored normative questions and ‘obliterated the distinction between men and brutes’.
The ‘decline’ was not the death of political theory but a temporary eclipse of its normative-philosophical dimension by positivism and ideology — the two causes

identified. Even Cobban conceded that ‘all was not yet lost’, and the fact that Easton himself launched the post-behavioural ‘Credo of Relevance’ in 1969 shows the decline was a self-correcting phase, not an end.
Q — Comment on the resurgence of political theory. Account for its revival since the 1970s. (UPSC 2019)
Explain how and why political theory came back — the trigger, the thinkers, and the new frontiers.
post-behavioural turn (1969) converted political science from a ‘pure’ to an ‘applied’ science and readmitted values.
: the two causes of decline (positivism + ideology) gave way; the grand tradition revived through
— the two camps borrowed from each other:
used an empirical device (the original position),
attacked Schumpeter and Dahl’s empirical democracy.
— feminism, human rights, environmentalism and subaltern justice reopened value-judgment.
(Climate: science measures the warming, only PT decides who must pay for it.)
— science supplies the means, philosophy the ends — complementary;
After being written off in the 1950s, political theory staged a strong resurgence from the 1970s. The turning point was

post-behavioural ‘Credo of Relevance’ (1969), which converted political science from a ‘pure’ into an ‘applied’ science, insisting that scientific enquiry help society tide over its crises and renewing concern with values.
Beyond Ideology: The Revival of Political Theory

, argued that the two causes of the earlier decline — the rise of positivism and the prevalence of ideologies culminating in Marxism — had given way, and that the grand tradition was again in the ascendant in the work of
Michael Oakeshott, Hannah Arendt, Bertrand de Jouvenel, Leo Strauss, Eric Voegelin and John Rawls
. For Germino, political theory must be identified with political philosophy — a critical study of the principles of right order.
The old dispute subsided as each camp borrowed from the other:
, an exponent of scientific method, drew conclusions about social values;
adopted an empirical device — the original position — to derive his principles of justice;
attacked the empirical theory of democracy of Schumpeter and Dahl with his own radical theory; and
brought empirical insight to the critique of capitalism.

Fresh concerns — environmentalism, feminism, human rights and social justice for subaltern groups — reopened the horizons of value-judgment, since indifference to value-judgment ‘will leave society in the dark’. Climate change is the sharpest illustration: science can measure the warming, but only political theory can decide who bears the burden of preventing it.

It is now held that political science strengthens our means while political philosophy determines our ends, the two playing complementary roles. The resurgence re-established political theory as a synthesis of empiricism and normativism;
is its paradigmatic fruit, confirming that political theory is ‘not dead’ but a practical, action-guiding activity.

contentText: Syllabus — Political Theory: meaning and approaches. (UPSC PSIR Paper-1A, Unit 1) Unit Snapshot What this unit covers:  meaning, nature, scope and contents of political theory; political theory as history / philosophy / science; the debate on the decline and resurgence of political theory; and approaches — Traditional (philosophical/normative, historical, empirical, legal, institutional), Modern (behavioural, post-behavioural, systems) and Contemporary/Other (postmodern, textual & contextual, deconstruction). Must-know thinkers:  Sabine, Catlin, Hacker, Leo Strauss, Dante Germino, David Easton, Alfred Cobban, Lipset, David Held, John Plamenatz, Van Dyke, Wallas, Bentley, Merriam, Skinner & Pocock, Derrida, Skocpol. PYQ trend:  near-annual. Decline (2018) & Resurgence (2019); Behavioural (2021), Post-Behavioural (2016), Normative (2020) and Systems (2022) approaches; nature/relevance of political theory (Plamenatz, 2014). Master Questions Q — “Political theory is not an escape mechanism but an arduous calling.” (Plamenatz) Examine the meaning, nature and relevance of political theory. (UPSC 2014) What it’s asking:  Define political theory → show what it is made of → prove it still matters. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Meaning  — PT both  explains  and  evaluates .  (Poverty: science asks “why are they poor?”, philosophy asks “should poverty exist?”)  —  Sabine : “anything about politics or relevant to politics.” 2. Nature  — history (facts) + philosophy (values) + science (explanation). Its 3 functions:  description  (India is a parliamentary democracy) →  criticism  (has it delivered equality to Dalits/women?) →  reconstruction  (complete it with social & economic democracy). 3. Theory ≠ Ideology  — theory investigates (“is this power just?”); ideology, like a party manifesto, justifies.  Hacker : the ideologue is an ‘interested party’. 4. Relevance  — settles what data cannot (reservation, euthanasia, AI judges) and yields a  theory of action  — reform / revolution / conservation.  Held : else politics is ‘left to the ignorant and self-interested’ →  Plamenatz’s  ‘arduous calling’. 5. Conclusion  — synthesis of facts and values;  Rawls  (1971) is the proof. Model Answer 1. Meaning.  Political theory is the systematic study of the political — the state, power, justice and the good society — which simultaneously  explains  and  evaluates . On poverty, for instance, it asks both why deprivation exists and whether a just society may tolerate it.  George Sabine  defines it broadly as “anything about politics or relevant to politics.” It is therefore neither pure philosophy nor pure science but an  ‘essentially mixed mode of thought’ . 2. Nature.  Its nature is a triple identity: it is  history  in so far as it rests on facts,  philosophy  in so far as it judges values, and  science  in so far as it explains — hence the theorist must be ‘part historian, part philosopher, part scientist’.  Catlin  and  Hacker  capture this as political science (what men and women actually DO) + political philosophy (what they OUGHT to do). Together these discharge three functions, best seen on Indian democracy:  description  — that India is a parliamentary democracy resting on universal adult franchise;  criticism  — whether that democracy has in fact secured equality for Dalits, women and the poor; and  reconstruction  — the prescription that political democracy be completed by social and economic democracy through affirmative action and empowered local self-government. 3. Theory versus ideology.  Hacker  cautions that theory must be kept distinct from ideology. A theory is dispassionate and disinterested, asking whether an arrangement of power is just; an ideology — like a party manifesto — begins by assuming its own side is right and reasons backwards, its author being an ‘interested party’. This distinction preserves political theory’s claim to objectivity. 4. Relevance.  Far from being escapist, political theory alone addresses questions no quantity of data can settle — reservation, euthanasia, the use of AI in adjudication. It yields not merely a theory of man or society but a  theory of action : reform (as through constitutional amendment), revolution (as in 1917), or conservation of the existing order.  David Held  warns that without its systematic pursuit, “politics will be left to the ignorant and self-interested, or to those simply with a ‘will to power’.” This is precisely why  Plamenatz  insists it is “not an escape mechanism but an arduous calling.” 5. Conclusion.  Political theory has grown from its normative past to its scientific present and now seeks a synthesis of history, philosophy and science, of normativism and empiricism. Its relevance lies in being a practical, action-guiding activity;  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  is its finest modern vindication. Q — Discuss the significance of the normative approach to political theory, situating it among the traditional approaches. (UPSC 2020) What it’s asking:  (a) What the normative approach is, and (b) why it matters against the other traditional approaches. Gist — the spine to recall 1. What an ‘approach’ is  — the lens you study politics through.  (One Parliament: a lawyer asks “is it constitutional?”, a historian “how did it evolve?”, a philosopher “is it just?”)  —  Van Dyke : the “criteria of selection”. 2. Normative  (Plato, Strauss) — asks what OUGHT to be. Two tasks:  clarifies concepts  (justice = equal income? opportunity? rights?) and  sets standards  (a ruler winning every election is  legal  — but  legitimate ?). 3. Other traditional  —  historical  (Locke backed liberty after absolute monarchy; Laski’s ‘child of his times’ — but Popper warns its determinist form, ‘historicism’, licenses tyranny);  empirical  (counts Dalit turnout, not whether caste is just);  legal-institutional  (may a Governor withhold assent to a Bill?). 4. Significance  — science gives the  means , philosophy the  ends .  (Engineering builds the car but can’t choose the destination; science builds AI but can’t say if AI may judge a human.) 5. Critique & revival  — dismissed as ‘arm-chair theory’, yet revived via the  Frankfurt School, communitarianism, multiculturalism . 6. Conclusion  — no single approach suffices;  Rawls’s  1970s revival settles its significance. Model Answer 1. What an approach is.  An approach is the lens through which politics is studied: examining one Parliament, the lawyer asks whether it is constitutional, the historian how it evolved, the philosopher whether it is just.  Vernon Van Dyke  therefore defines an approach as the  “criteria of selection”  — the standards governing which problems and which data we admit — as distinct from  method , which is merely the procedure for gathering data. The traditional approaches are those that dominated before the behavioural revolution of the 1950s. 2. The normative approach.  Associated with  Plato  and, in our times,  Leo Strauss , it is prescriptive, asking not why people are poor but whether society  ought  to permit poverty. It performs two tasks. First, it  clarifies concepts : ‘justice’ may mean equal income to a socialist, equal opportunity to a liberal, or merely equal rights to a libertarian — analysis is needed before argument. Second, it  evolves ‘standards of right and wrong’  to judge institutions: a ruler who wins every election may be perfectly legal, yet the normative theorist still asks whether his rule is legitimate. For  Strauss , political science and political philosophy are coterminous — facts  and  values are indispensable. 3. Other traditional approaches.  The  historical  ( Sabine, Machiavelli ) explains ideas by their age — Locke championed liberty because he wrote in the shadow of absolute monarchy;  Laski : “every thinker is the child of his times.” Its determinist form, which  Popper  brands  ‘historicism’ , is dangerous: the claim that capitalism must  inevitably  collapse can be used to justify totalitarian means. The  empirical  ( Aristotle, Locke ) records ‘what is’ — the share of Dalits who voted, not whether caste is just. The  legal-institutional  ( Wheare, Dicey, Jennings ) asks whether a Governor may withhold assent to a Bill, studying the constitution and organs of government, but relies on description rather than explanation. 4. Significance.  The normative approach keeps values at the centre of the discipline. Empirical enquiry ‘strengthens our means’, but we must resort to political philosophy ‘to determine our ends’ — engineering can build the car, but never choose the destination. Science can construct artificial intelligence; only normative theory can decide whether it may sit in judgment on a human being. 5. Critique and revival.  Critics dismiss it as biased, divorced from reality and ‘arm-chair theory’ incapable of scientific test. Yet it revived powerfully through the  Frankfurt School, communitarianism, multiculturalism and postmodernism , proving the questions it raises cannot be abandoned. 6. Conclusion.  No single approach can capture the complexity of the discipline; a combination is required.  Rawls’s  revival of normative justice in the 1970s — an outcome of the post-behavioural upsurge — is the clearest proof of its enduring significance. Instead of asking what the Constitution prescribes, it asks why a particular voter chose a particular party — dissolving formal institutions into ‘systems’ and ‘processes’ to focus on the conduct of real actors. 2. Roots and tenets.  Though it flourished among American scholars after the Second World War, it began with  Graham Wallas  ( Human Nature in Politics ) and  Arthur Bentley  ( The Process of Government ), both 1908, and was advanced by  Charles Merriam  (the Chicago School) and  G.E.G. Catlin  (a value-free science of power).  David Easton  systematised it in  eight tenets  — regularities, systematisation, technique, measurement, verification, integration, value-neutrality and pure science. 3. Importance.  Behaviouralism arrested the decline of the discipline. It pioneered the study of  electoral behaviour , giving parties a scientific basis for strategy; it clarified the gap between theory and practice, as elitists and pluralists tested the reality of democracy in the West; and it made  comparative politics  a major field by showing that in developing societies ‘text differs from context’ — the Constitution promises equality while the village practises caste — so legal-institutional study alone was inadequate. 4. Decline — the attack on value-neutrality.  Traditionalists, above all  Leo Strauss , argued that a value-free science destroys the distinction between higher and lower ends: ignoring values is like “making no difference between pure water and dirty water.” Others denied that regularities are even possible in human conduct, since the same person may not behave alike twice in like conditions. 5. Decline — technique over purpose.  By chasing measurement and method, behaviouralism sacrificed both the scope and the relevance of the subject.  Easton  himself conceded that scholars were “sitting in ivory towers, perfecting their techniques” while ignoring the purposes they served. The upheavals of the 1950s–60s — civil rights, the women’s movement, Vietnam — exposed a discipline with nothing to offer policymakers, triggering the post-behavioural revolution of 1969. 6. Conclusion.  Behaviouralism was a necessary corrective that made political science rigorous and empirical; but its indifference to values produced a ‘second decline’, out of which post-behaviouralism emerged as a synthesis rather than a rejection. Q — Comment on the post-behavioural approach. “It is a synthesis of tradition and behaviouralism.” (UPSC 2016) What it’s asking:  Explain the ‘Credo of Relevance’ and show why it is a synthesis, not a rejection, of behaviouralism. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Origin  —  Easton’s  1969 APSA address, the  ‘Credo of Relevance’ , reacting to behaviouralism’s silence during the 1960s crises. 2. Core slogan  — “better to be vague than non-relevantly precise”;  creative theory = Action + Relevance . 3. Features  — invites values back; theory must solve crises; political science is  applied , not pure; the scholar’s responsibility exceeds the natural scientist’s. 4. Why a synthesis  — traditionalism (thesis) + behaviouralism (antithesis) → post-behaviouralism (synthesis); it keeps the behavioural method but adds purpose.  (Keep the microscope — but study disease, not dust.) 5. Conclusion  — reconciled facts and values → paved the way for the resurgence;  Rawls  (1971) is its finest fruit. Model Answer 1. Origin.  Post-behaviouralism was launched by  David Easton  in his 1969 presidential address to the American Political Science Association, the  ‘Credo of Relevance’ . It arose from dissatisfaction with a discipline that had perfected its instruments while remaining silent on the civil-rights, anti-war and women’s movements convulsing American society. 2. Core slogan.  Its watchword was that “it is better to be vague than non-relevantly precise.” Easton called for a  ‘creative theory’  resting on two parameters —  Action  and  Relevance : research must be chosen for its usefulness to society, not for the elegance of its method. 3. Features.  Easton’s features follow from this: it does not reject values but  invites  them; theory must have the capacity to solve crises; it should promote values that help civilisation flourish; political science is an  applied , not a pure, science; and the social scientist’s responsibility is greater than the natural scientist’s. 4. Why it is a synthesis.  Traditionalism is the thesis, behaviouralism the antithesis, and post-behaviouralism the  synthesis . Crucially it is  not  a rejection of behaviouralism: its assumptions, methods and approaches remain the same, and only two things change — technique may be compromised for the sake of relevance, and values are readmitted. It keeps the microscope, but insists on studying disease rather than dust. Where behaviouralism sought pure knowledge, micro-level and indifferent to change, post-behaviouralism seeks applied knowledge, macro-level and committed to social problem-solving. 5. Conclusion.  By restoring the normative dimension without abandoning scientific method, post-behaviouralism reconciled facts and values and paved the way for the resurgence of political theory.  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971) , an outcome of the post-behavioural upsurge, is the finest example of such ‘creative theory’. Q — “Political theory is dead.” Critically examine the debate on the decline of political theory. What, according to David Easton, were its causes? (UPSC 2018) What it’s asking:  State the ‘death’ charge → give Easton’s four causes → add the other critics → judge whether it really died. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The charge  —  Easton ,  The Political System (1953) : traditional PT is ‘mere speculation’, devoid of observation of political reality. 2. Historicism  — living ‘parasitically on ideas a century old’.  (Teaching Plato and Aristotle while unable to explain the rise of fascism.) 3. Moral relativism  — values excluded in the chase for a value-neutral science. 4. Science-theory confusion + hyper-factualism  — method given primacy over purpose;  Catlin’s  “we want facts, facts and facts” →  Easton’s  ‘theoretical malnutrition and a surfeit of facts’. 5. Other critics  —  Cobban  (irrelevant in both capitalist and communist systems),  Lipset  (the ‘good society’ already achieved in the US),  Strauss  (positivism ‘obliterates the distinction between men and brutes’). 6. Conclusion  — not death but an eclipse of the normative side; even Cobban said ‘all was not yet lost’, and Easton himself launched the revival in 1969. Model Answer 1. The charge.  In the 1950s the exponents of the ‘new science of politics’ declared traditional political theory to be in decline.  David Easton , in  The Political System: An Inquiry into the State of Political Science (1953) , asserted that it rested on “mere speculation” and was devoid of acute observation of political reality; to lay scientific foundations, politics had to be rescued from the study of the classics. 2. Historicism.  Easton’s first cause: historicists such as  Sabine  and  Dunning  dwelt on century-old ideas, making the discipline ‘parasitic’ and blind to contemporary problems — political scientists were expounding Plato and Aristotle while unable to account for the rise of fascism or communism. 3. Moral relativism.  The second cause was the exclusion of value from political theory in pursuit of the empirical scientist’s value-neutrality. Easton himself did not favour abandoning values altogether: a value system sensitive to society’s problems is necessary, and its abandonment in the name of science impoverished the discipline. 4. Science-theory confusion and hyper-factualism.  The third cause was the over-reliance on scientific method, whereby  method was given primacy over purpose . The fourth was  hyper-factualism  — an obsession with facts and information, captured in  Catlin’s  “we want facts, facts and facts.” Political scientists grew adept at measuring opinion and voting yet gave their research no theoretical dimension, a condition Easton called ‘theoretical malnutrition and a surfeit of facts’. 5. Other critics.  Alfred Cobban  (in  The Decline of Political Theory ) argued theory had lost significance in capitalist systems dominated by bureaucracy and in communist systems ruled by a party oligarchy.  Seymour Martin Lipset  (in  Political Man ) claimed the age-old search for the ‘good society’ had ended in the United States, which was “the closest approximation to the good society in operation.”  Leo Strauss  replied that the new science of politics was itself a symptom of decline: by adopting positivism it ignored normative questions and ‘obliterated the distinction between men and brutes’. 6. Conclusion.  The ‘decline’ was not the death of political theory but a temporary eclipse of its normative-philosophical dimension by positivism and ideology — the two causes  Germino  identified. Even Cobban conceded that ‘all was not yet lost’, and the fact that Easton himself launched the post-behavioural ‘Credo of Relevance’ in 1969 shows the decline was a self-correcting phase, not an end. Q — Comment on the resurgence of political theory. Account for its revival since the 1970s. (UPSC 2019) What it’s asking:  Explain how and why political theory came back — the trigger, the thinkers, and the new frontiers. Gist — the spine to recall 1. Trigger  —  Easton’s  post-behavioural turn (1969) converted political science from a ‘pure’ to an ‘applied’ science and readmitted values. 2. Revival of philosophy  —  Germino ,  Beyond Ideology : the two causes of decline (positivism + ideology) gave way; the grand tradition revived through  Oakeshott, Arendt, Strauss, Rawls . 3. Convergence  — the two camps borrowed from each other:  Popper  drew value conclusions,  Rawls  used an empirical device (the original position),  Macpherson  attacked Schumpeter and Dahl’s empirical democracy. 4. New frontiers  — feminism, human rights, environmentalism and subaltern justice reopened value-judgment.  (Climate: science measures the warming, only PT decides who must pay for it.) 5. Conclusion  — science supplies the means, philosophy the ends — complementary;  Rawls  (1971) proves PT is ‘not dead’. Model Answer 1. Trigger.  After being written off in the 1950s, political theory staged a strong resurgence from the 1970s. The turning point was  David Easton’s  post-behavioural ‘Credo of Relevance’ (1969), which converted political science from a ‘pure’ into an ‘applied’ science, insisting that scientific enquiry help society tide over its crises and renewing concern with values. 2. Revival of political philosophy.  Dante Germino , in  Beyond Ideology: The Revival of Political Theory , argued that the two causes of the earlier decline — the rise of positivism and the prevalence of ideologies culminating in Marxism — had given way, and that the grand tradition was again in the ascendant in the work of  Michael Oakeshott, Hannah Arendt, Bertrand de Jouvenel, Leo Strauss, Eric Voegelin and John Rawls . For Germino, political theory must be identified with political philosophy — a critical study of the principles of right order. 3. Convergence of science and philosophy.  The old dispute subsided as each camp borrowed from the other:  Karl Popper , an exponent of scientific method, drew conclusions about social values;  John Rawls  adopted an empirical device — the original position — to derive his principles of justice;  C.B. Macpherson  attacked the empirical theory of democracy of Schumpeter and Dahl with his own radical theory; and  Marcuse  and  Habermas  brought empirical insight to the critique of capitalism. 4. New frontiers.  Fresh concerns — environmentalism, feminism, human rights and social justice for subaltern groups — reopened the horizons of value-judgment, since indifference to value-judgment ‘will leave society in the dark’. Climate change is the sharpest illustration: science can measure the warming, but only political theory can decide who bears the burden of preventing it. 5. Conclusion.  It is now held that political science strengthens our means while political philosophy determines our ends, the two playing complementary roles. The resurgence re-established political theory as a synthesis of empiricism and normativism;  Rawls’s   A Theory of Justice (1971)  is its paradigmatic fruit, confirming that political theory is ‘not dead’ but a practical, action-guiding activity. Q — Comment on the systems approach to the study of politics, and situate it among the other modern and contemporary approaches. (UPSC 2022) What it’s asking:  Explain Easton’s systems model → evaluate it → place it beside the other modern/contemporary approaches. Gist — the spine to recall 1. The model  — politics =  inputs  (demands + supports) →  conversion  (the ‘black box’) →  outputs  (decisions/policy) →  feedback .  (Farmers demand MSP → Cabinet and Parliament process it → a law issues → reactions feed back as fresh demands.) 2. Core definition  — the political system performs the  ‘authoritative allocation of values’  for a society. 3. Strengths  — holistic, comparative and self-regulating; dissolves formal institutions into systems and processes. 4. Critique  — abstract and  status-quoist  (it privileges equilibrium over conflict and change), Eurocentric, and neglects power, ideology and the individual. 5. Other contemporary approaches  — textual vs contextual ( Skinner & Pocock  read Locke’s ‘trust’ as his contemporaries did);  Derrida’s  deconstruction — “no meaning is ultimate.” 6. Conclusion  — no single approach captures politics;  Skocpol’s  ‘bringing the state back in’ shows a combination is needed. Model Answer 1. The model.  Among the modern approaches, the  systems approach  — pioneered by  David Easton  — was the most influential attempt to build a general, macro-level theory of the political process. Politics is modelled as a cycle:  inputs  of demands and supports flow from society; these undergo  conversion  within the political system (the ‘black box’);  outputs  emerge as authoritative decisions and policies; and  feedback  regenerates fresh demands, allowing the system to persist. Farmers press for a higher MSP, the Cabinet and Parliament process the claim, a policy issues, and the response to it returns as new demands. 2. Core definition.  Easton treats the political system as the set of interactions, abstracted from society, that carries out the  ‘authoritative allocation of values’  for that society — the most widely used definition of politics in the discipline. 3. Strengths.  It gave political science a holistic, comparative and self-regulating model, dissolving formal institutions into ‘systems’ and ‘processes’ so that attention shifts to the actual behaviour of political actors, and enabling states with very different institutions to be compared on a common framework. 4. Critique.  It is criticised as overly abstract and  status-quoist : by privileging system-persistence and equilibrium it underplays conflict, revolution and change. It is also Eurocentric and poorly suited to developing societies, and it neglects power, ideology and the individual — precisely what Marxist and Foucauldian analyses foreground. 5. Other contemporary approaches.  Classics such as  Plato’s Republic  and  Machiavelli’s The Prince  are read two ways: the  textual  approach seeks a literal, universal meaning, while the  contextual  approach interprets them for present situations. The Cambridge School —  Skinner and Pocock  — insists on the linguistic context, so that to grasp Locke’s use of ‘trust’ we must know how his contemporaries used the word.  Jacques Derrida’s  deconstruction  goes further: a text permits multiple readings, and “no meaning can be regarded as ultimate — every understanding can be a misunderstanding.” 6. Conclusion.  The proliferation of approaches — traditional, behavioural, post-behavioural, systems, textual/contextual and deconstruction — shows that no single approach can capture the complexity and veracity of the discipline. As  Theda Skocpol  urged in ‘bringing the state back in’, a combination of approaches is required to keep political theory relevant.
